tasks.description: Given name = 'Alice' and age = 30, print: 'My name is Alice and I am 30 years old.' using an f-string.
tasks.hint:
f-strings start with `f` before the opening quote: `f'...'`
Embed variables in `{}`: `f'My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.'`
Any valid Python expression works inside `{}` — variables, math, function calls.
tasks.expected: My name is Alice and I am 30 years old.
tasks.solution:
name = 'Alice'
age = 30
print(f'My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.')
tasks.walkthrough:
Two placeholders, each replaced by the value of the named variable.
The `f` prefix is what makes the braces active.

tasks.description: Use an f-string to print: '10 squared is 100' — compute 10**2 directly inside the f-string.
tasks.hint:
f-strings evaluate expressions inside `{}`, not just variable names.
`f'{10} squared is {10**2}'` → `'10 squared is 100'`
The calculation happens at runtime — very handy for inline computations.
tasks.walkthrough: The braces can hold expressions, not just names. `10 ** 2` is evaluated to 100 as the string is built.

tasks.description: Print the float 3.14159265 formatted to exactly 2 decimal places using an f-string format spec.
tasks.hint:
Format specs go inside `{}` after a colon: `f'{value:.2f}'`
`.2f` means: fixed-point notation with exactly 2 decimal places.
`f'{3.14159265:.2f}'` → `'3.14'` — it rounds automatically.
tasks.walkthrough:
The part after the colon is a format spec. `.2f` means fixed-point with two digits after the decimal point.
The value is rounded to 3.14 for display.

tasks.description: Print the number 42 padded to a width of 8 characters, right-aligned, with spaces on the left.
tasks.hint:
Right-align format spec: `f'{value:>8}'` — `>` means right, `8` is total width.
`f'{42:>8}'` → `'      42'` (6 spaces then 42)
Left-align uses `<`, centre uses `^`.
tasks.walkthrough:
`>8` means right-align inside a field 8 characters wide.
42 is two characters, so six spaces are added on the left.

tasks.description: Print a table header: 'Name       | Score' then two rows: 'Alice      | 95' and 'Bob        | 87'. Use f-strings with fixed widths.
tasks.hint:
Left-align in a fixed-width field: `f'{name:<10}'` — `<` is left-align, `10` is width.
`f'{name:<10}| {score}'` aligns the name column to 10 chars wide.
Repeat the same format for the header and both data rows.
tasks.walkthrough:
`<11` pads each name on the right to exactly 11 characters, so the `|` lands in the same column every time.
Count the spaces in the expected output carefully: Name plus seven spaces is 11 characters. The hint says 10, which is one short.
Double quotes are used inside the braces because the string itself uses single quotes.

tasks.description: Given price = 1234.567, print it formatted with a comma as thousands separator and 2 decimal places: '1,234.57'
tasks.hint:
The `,` in the format spec adds comma separators every 3 digits.
Combine with `.2f`: `f'{price:,.2f}'` → `'1,234.57'`
This is essential for displaying money and large numbers readably.
tasks.walkthrough:
The comma in the spec inserts a thousands separator. The `.2f` fixes two decimal places.
Together they turn 1234.567 into 1,234.57.

tasks.description: Use a multi-line string (triple quotes) to store and print a 3-line poem of your choice.
tasks.hint:
Triple-quoted strings preserve newlines and indentation exactly as written.
`text = """Line 1\nLine 2\nLine 3"""`  or write it on separate lines inside the triple quotes.
`print(text)` outputs it with the line breaks intact.
tasks.solution:
poem = '''The kettle hums,
the window fogs,
tea for one.'''
print(poem)
tasks.walkthrough:
Triple quotes let the string run across several lines without any `\n` characters.
Each line break inside the quotes becomes a line break in the output. Write your own poem; any three lines will do.

lesson.intro:
You've used f-strings to drop a variable into text. They can do more: line things
up in columns, fix the number of decimal places, add thousands separators. This is
the difference between output that's readable and output that isn't.

sections.heading: Expressions inside the braces
sections.body:
Anything that produces a value can go inside `{}`: a variable, some maths, a
function call, a method call.
sections.code:
name = 'Alice'
print(f'{name} has {len(name)} letters')
print(f'{10} squared is {10 ** 2}')
print(f'{name.upper()}!')
sections.output:
Alice has 5 letters
10 squared is 100
ALICE!

sections.heading: Format specs: a colon then instructions
sections.body:
After the value, a colon starts a format spec. `.2f` means two decimal places.
`,` adds thousands separators. They can be combined.

sections.heading: Width and alignment
sections.body:
A number in the spec sets a minimum width. `<` aligns left, `>` right,
`^` centre. Padding is done with spaces. This is how you make columns line up.

sections.heading: Multi-line strings
sections.body:
Three quotes start a string that can span several lines. The line breaks are
kept exactly as you typed them.
sections.code:
poem = '''Roses are red,
violets are blue,
this string has three lines,
and so does this too.'''
print(poem)
sections.output:
Roses are red,
violets are blue,
this string has three lines,
and so does this too.

watch_out: Forgetting the `f` before the quote. Without it, `{name}` is printed literally.
Using the same quote type inside the braces as around the string. `f'{d['key']}'` breaks; use `f"{d['key']}"`.
`:.2f` rounds for display only. The variable still holds the full value.
The width in `{name:<10}` is a minimum. Longer text isn't cut off, it just pushes the column over.
